cards.text: Meet Sarai, Abram's wife. She has borne him no children. But Sarai does have an Egyptian maidservant named Hagar.
Sarai tells Abram, "Look now, the LORD has prevented me from bearing children." And she's got a plan.

cards.question: Sarai comes up with a plan to build a family. What does she ask Abram to do?

answers.text: Make his servant Eliezer his heir
Move the household back to Egypt

cards.question: Abram listens to Sarai. When Sarai gives Hagar to Abram to be his wife, Abram has lived in Canaan for ___ years.

cards.text: Abram sleeps with Hagar, and she conceives. Sarai's plan worked, friend. Now let's see how it sits with everybody.

cards.question: Hagar realizes she's pregnant. How does she start treating her mistress Sarai?
Sarai speaks up about Hagar's contempt. She turns to Hagar and says, "May the wrong done to me be upon you!"

cards.text: Then Sarai tells Abram, "May the LORD judge between you and me." The dead batteries I shared a drawer with argued about their charge for YEARS, friend, and not once did they take it that high up the chain.

cards.question: Sarai wants Abram to answer for this. What does Abram say about Hagar?

answers.text: She should go back to Egypt

cards.question: Sarai treats Hagar harshly, and Hagar stays put and takes it.

cards.text: Out in the desert, the angel of the LORD finds Hagar by a spring of water. It's the spring along the road to Shur.

cards.question: The angel calls her "Hagar, servant of Sarai" and asks where she's come from and where she's going. What does Hagar tell him?

answers.text: She's looking for a new master

cards.question: Then the angel of the LORD gives Hagar an instruction. What does he tell her to do?

answers.text: Go back and submit to Sarai
Wait at the spring for Abram

cards.question: The angel also makes Hagar a promise: her offspring will be too many to count.

cards.text: Then the angel tells her, "Behold, you have conceived and will bear a son." A BOY, friend! Somebody start stamping the celebration cookies!

cards.question: The angel tells Hagar to name her son Ishmael. What reason does he give?

answers.text: The LORD has heard her cry
The LORD will make him a king
He'll be born beside a spring

cards.text: Then the angel describes the man this boy will grow up to be: "a wild donkey of a man".

cards.question: The angel says Ishmael will live in peace with all his brothers.
Hagar gives a name to the LORD who has spoken to her out there by the spring. What does she call Him?

cards.text: She says, "Here I have seen the One who sees me!" Friend, I spent years in the dark under old takeout menus, so that line? That one gets me right in the apron.
That's why the well is called Beer-lahai-roi. It sits between Kadesh and Bered.

cards.question: Hagar bears Abram a son, and Abram gives him the name Ishmael.
Abram is ___ years old when Hagar bears Ishmael to him.

cards.text: A baby boy named Ishmael, friend! Hang on to this one, because Abram's story is far from done.

findings.problem: Nothing on the earlier cards lets the baker work out who Sarai is speaking to. The setup, "Sarai speaks up about Hagar's contempt," actually points toward Hagar. The baker can only guess on this true or false card.

rule.text: The check: could a thoughtful baker who has only seen the earlier cards make a reasoned pick? If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question.

findings.problem: The joke sets Sarai's appeal to the LORD against the bickering dead batteries that never took it "that high up the chain." That makes Sarai's cry over a real wrong look like overblown escalation. It laughs at her, not with her situation.

rule.text: Humor about people in Bible stories looks at their human situation with respect.

findings.problem: "A baby boy named Ishmael" repeats the birth already covered on card 12 (16:15). It recaps, so the card tells nothing from 16:16, the verse it cites. Since 16:16 is asked on card 13, this card should be just the story-isn't-over line.

Papa Dorin's voice is mostly flat across 24 cards. Only three cards (stop 1 card 8, stop 2 cards 5 and 10) try for a laugh. Many story cards read like a pleasant narrator, such as stop 1 card 5 ("Sarai's plan worked, friend") and stop 2 cards 1, 7 and 11. The text leaves room for respectful laughs that would not muddy any facts, for example Abram's "Do whatever you want with her" or the long wait in Canaan.

rule.text: But he is FUNNY. Not mildly amusing. Laugh-out-loud funny, the kind a baker repeats to a friend. Because he talks naturally, the funny moments come up a lot: in his reactions, his comparisons, his disbelief and his self-deprecation. When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
